answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text: ABC feels that the primary benefits of developing and using consequential accounting methods for electricity-sector actions is that it provides a mechanism for highlighting projects and procurement decisions that drive system-level decarbonization outside of pure emissions ownership. The challenge is ensuring that it is critical to structure the accounting in such a way that it truly incentivizes those most impactful projects in a technology-agnostic way. Historically, carbon accounting and target-setting frameworks have disadvantaged impactful decarbonization solutions like renewable gases and clean fuels. It is for those reasons that the proposed consequential methods present significant challenges. Results are highly sensitive to assumptions about counterfactuals, deliverability, quality criteria, etc., which can vary by region and over time and are often difficult to validate. Without clear methodological guardrails and standardized claims guidance that is informed by science and experts within the renewable gases and clean fuels space, there is a risk that consequential results could be misinterpreted and lead to confusion or understated impact.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text: ABC agrees the proposed Scope 2 TWG subgroup formula is structurally appropriate for quantifying emissions impacts from electricity projects, as it clearly distinguishes between project activity, counterfactual grid emissions, and project emissions. This difference-based structure can consistently capture system-level impacts across technologies, including dispatchable resources such as biogas-to-electricity, provided that underlying assumptions and parameters are robustly defined.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text: ABC agrees that including secondary effects provides a more complete view of the system-level emissions impact of electricity projects, particularly for dispatchable, low-carbon resources like biogas-to-electricity. Biogas generation can reduce reliance on high-emission peaker plants and influence future grid investment decisions, such as delaying new fossil capacity, which would not be captured by primary effects alone. Accounting for these indirect impacts better reflects the true marginal climate benefits of biogas projects and aligns reported emissions impacts with the real-world decarbonization they enable. Examples of these secondary effects that should be considered include displacement of high-emission marginal generators during peak hours, avoided future fossil capacity build, methane reductions from feedstocks, and shifts in market dispatch or system reliability. These can be quantified using marginal emissions factors, lifecycle emissions for feedstocks, scenario modeling of future capacity, or market simulation of dispatch impacts. Including these effects provides a more accurate representation of the true system-level climate benefits of biogas-to-electricity projects.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text: ABC supports requiring a regulatory test as an essential way to preserve the integrity of additionality claims. Actions already mandated by law or regulation would occur regardless of voluntary incentives and therefore should not be credited as additional. This principle is already embedded across major climate disclosure frameworks and standards, helping ensure consistency, comparability, and credibility of claims. Without a regulatory test, there is a risk of overstating climate impact by crediting compliance activities rather than truly incentive-driven actions. In addition, ABC suggests that timing tests can be helpful in some cases, but they should not be required in all situations. Thus, ABC advocates that the timing test is optional. Large projects like biogas and renewable fuels can take years to plan and develop, and early steps are often taken before it’s clear whether a project can actually be financed or built. A strict timing rule could exclude projects that still depend on long-term buyers or incentives to move forward.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text: As outlined in the earlier response, ABC is supportive of and notes that the regulatory test is an appropriate gauge of additionality and is already widely used. Therefore, we agree that it is feasible to implement as a part of the consequential accounting framework. Furthermore, although ABC does not agree that any of the following should be required, that due to their optional/partial use in other frameworks and in the event they are well-defined and regularly updated that tests such as positive lists and common practice would be slightly more feasible and scalable. Whereas, tests such as financial analysis, contractual/tenor, strict timing, barrier, and first-of-its-kind tests will be far more complex and least feasible to implement consistently due to high data requirements, subjectivity, and misalignment with real-world project development. Therefore, ABC reinforces the position that these should not be required.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text: ABC recommends the national (country) level as the maximum appropriate spatial boundary for marginal emission rates. This boundary captures system-level emissions impacts while remaining practical and globally applicable. More granular boundaries, such as grid regions or local zones, may be used optionally by reporting entities where high-quality data and regional circumstances allow, consistent with ABC’s position in Scope 2 accounting that boundaries should balance accuracy with feasibility and flexibility.
